items.prompt: What does a transaction guarantee about the operations inside it?
choices: They run faster than normal
They all happen, or none of them do
They always run in isolation from other operations
They are automatically logged for auditing
items.explanation: A transaction's core guarantee is all-or-nothing: either every operation inside it happens, or none of them do.

items.prompt: In the scenario, placing an order does two things. What are they?
choices: Decrement stock, then insert the order record
Insert the order record, then charge the customer
Validate the customer, then decrement stock
Insert the order record twice
items.explanation: L1's scenario is exactly two writes: decrement the product's stock, then insert a new order record.

items.prompt: Which step failed in L1's scenario?
choices: Step 1, the stock decrement
Step 2, the order insert
Both steps failed
Neither step failed
items.explanation: The stock decrement (step 1) succeeded; the order insert (step 2) failed a moment later.

items.prompt: Was the stock decrement itself buggy code?
choices: Yes, it had an off-by-one error
No — it ran exactly as intended; the problem is elsewhere
Yes, it ran twice
No, because stock was never actually decremented
items.explanation: Neither individual write was wrong. The stock decrement really did need to happen; the bug is structural, not in either line.

items.prompt: What is a 'rollback', in plain words?
choices: Undoing changes already made because the whole action didn't finish safely
Running the same write twice to be sure
Logging an error message
Decrementing stock a second time
items.explanation: Rollback means undoing every change made so far because the whole action did not finish safely.

items.prompt: What is 'commit', in plain words?
choices: The point where a transaction's changes become permanent and visible
The moment a request is first received
The step where stock is decremented
A synonym for rollback
items.explanation: Commit is the single moment a transaction's changes become permanent and visible, once everything succeeded.

items.prompt: Is 'partially done' a hypothetical state, or a real one a system can be left in without transactions?
choices: Purely hypothetical, databases prevent this automatically
A real, reachable state if writes can fail independently of each other
Only possible if the server is literally out of memory
Only possible in test environments
items.explanation: If two writes can fail independently, 'partially done' is a real, reachable state — exactly what happened in the scenario.

items.prompt: Which of these best completes: 'A transaction is a way of saying these operations ___'
choices: either all happen, or none of them do
run on separate threads
always finish within 1 second
only ever read data, never write it
items.explanation: That's the defining promise of a transaction: all-or-nothing.

items.prompt: A system has 3 writes instead of 2 — stock, order, and loyalty points — but only writes 1 and 2 are wrapped in a transaction; write 3 runs separately afterward. Is the partial-write bug from L1 now fully eliminated?
choices: Yes, any transaction wrapping at all removes the risk
No — write 3 can still be left out if it fails independently, so the system can still end up partially done, just one write later
Yes, because loyalty points don't affect stock
No, because transactions can only wrap exactly 2 operations
items.explanation: Wrapping only some of the related writes in a transaction leaves the same structural gap for whatever's left outside it.
items.reflection: The stock/order bug is really about splitting one logical action into pieces that can fail independently. Where else have you seen a single "thing that happened" get split into multiple steps that can get out of sync with each other — a form that saves to a draft and then submits separately, a delivery that's marked "shipped" before payment actually clears?

items.prompt: Someone argues the order-insert bug was really 'a bug in the order-insert code' and should be fixed by making that one function retry on failure. Why does that framing miss the actual lesson?
choices: Because retrying always makes things worse
Because the real issue is structural — nothing treated the two writes as one unit, so even a retry-fixed insert leaves the same gap for the next multi-write action elsewhere
Because order inserts should never be retried under any circumstances
Because the stock decrement was the actual buggy step, not the insert
items.explanation: Patching this one bug doesn't fix the structural gap — the next multi-write action without a transaction boundary has the identical problem.
items.reflection: The stock/order bug is really about splitting one logical action into pieces that can fail independently. Where else have you seen a single "thing that happened" get split into multiple steps that can get out of sync with each other — a form that saves to a draft and then submits separately, a delivery that's marked "shipped" before payment actually clears?

items.prompt: Suppose the order insert actually succeeded on the server, but the HTTP response telling the client 'success' got lost in transit, so the client thinks it failed and retries. Is this the same partial-write problem that transactions solve?
choices: Yes, identical — the stock and order data are left inconsistent
No — the server's data is internally consistent (both writes happened); this is a different problem, about the client and server disagreeing on the outcome of an already-complete action
Yes, because the client's retry will always double the stock decrement
No, because HTTP responses can never be lost
items.explanation: The server's own data is fine here — both writes landed. This is a communication/idempotency problem, a different shape than a partial write.
items.reflection: The stock/order bug is really about splitting one logical action into pieces that can fail independently. Where else have you seen a single "thing that happened" get split into multiple steps that can get out of sync with each other — a form that saves to a draft and then submits separately, a delivery that's marked "shipped" before payment actually clears?

items.prompt: What do the four letters in ACID stand for?
choices: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Availability, Concurrency, Integrity, Durability
Atomicity, Concurrency, Isolation, Dependency
Accuracy, Consistency, Independence, Durability
items.explanation: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

items.prompt: Which ACID property means 'all-or-nothing'?
choices: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
items.explanation: Atomicity is the all-or-nothing guarantee: every operation happens, or none do.

items.prompt: Which ACID property means data-level rules always hold?
choices: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
items.explanation: Consistency guarantees data-level invariants hold true before and after a transaction.

items.prompt: Which ACID property means concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-finished work?
choices: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
items.explanation: Isolation is specifically about concurrent transactions not seeing each other's unfinished work.

items.prompt: Which ACID property means a successful result survives a crash right after?
choices: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
items.explanation: Durability guarantees a reported success survives a crash immediately afterward.

items.prompt: According to L1, what does Durability guarantee?
choices: The transaction runs faster than non-durable code
Once a transaction reports success, that result survives a crash immediately afterward
The data is encrypted at rest
The transaction can be undone at any later time
items.explanation: Durability is specifically about a reported success surviving an immediately following crash.

items.prompt: 'Can another request see my half-finished work?' is the one-breath question for which property?
choices: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
items.explanation: That's Isolation's defining question.

items.prompt: 'Did the whole action finish, or do we undo it?' is the one-breath question for which property?
choices: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
items.explanation: That's Atomicity's defining question.

items.prompt: A transaction correctly rolls back every half-finished write on failure (true all-or-nothing behavior), but two transactions running at the same time can still read each other's uncommitted data. Which ACID property is missing here, and is Atomicity enough to call this system ACID-compliant?
choices: Nothing is missing — atomicity alone is sufficient for ACID
Isolation is missing, and no — atomicity only guarantees each transaction's own all-or-nothing behavior, not how two concurrent transactions interact
Consistency is missing, because atomicity implies isolation automatically
Durability is missing, because atomicity and durability are the same guarantee
items.explanation: Atomicity and Isolation are separate guarantees — a system can have flawless all-or-nothing behavior per transaction while still letting transactions interfere with each other.
items.reflection: ACID packages four separate guarantees under one acronym because systems historically got some of them right while missing others — a cache might be durable but not atomic, a naive script might be atomic but not isolated. Think of a tool or process you use (not a database) that gives you some but not all four of these guarantees — which one is missing, and what goes wrong when it's missing?

items.prompt: A transaction commits successfully, is reported to the user as a success, and five seconds later the server crashes. On restart, that change is gone. Which specific ACID guarantee was violated?
choices: Atomicity — the transaction wasn't fully undone
Consistency — an invariant was broken
Durability — a reported success didn't survive a crash
Isolation — another transaction interfered
items.explanation: This is exactly Durability's job: a reported success must survive a crash immediately after. Here it didn't.
items.reflection: ACID packages four separate guarantees under one acronym because systems historically got some of them right while missing others — a cache might be durable but not atomic, a naive script might be atomic but not isolated. Think of a tool or process you use (not a database) that gives you some but not all four of these guarantees — which one is missing, and what goes wrong when it's missing?

items.prompt: A banking system transfers money by debiting account A and crediting account B inside a transaction, but allows the transaction to commit even if the total of A+B changes (a bug in the math). Which ACID property is this system failing to enforce, even though atomicity, isolation, and durability are all implemented correctly?
choices: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
items.explanation: A data-level rule (the combined total must be preserved) is being violated — that's specifically Consistency's job, independent of the other three.
items.reflection: ACID packages four separate guarantees under one acronym because systems historically got some of them right while missing others — a cache might be durable but not atomic, a naive script might be atomic but not isolated. Think of a tool or process you use (not a database) that gives you some but not all four of these guarantees — which one is missing, and what goes wrong when it's missing?

items.prompt: What is a 'commit', as defined in L1?
choices: Making a transaction's changes permanent and visible, only once every operation has succeeded
Starting a new transaction
Undoing a transaction's changes
Logging a transaction for later review
items.explanation: Commit makes a transaction's changes permanent and visible, and only happens once every operation has succeeded.

items.prompt: What is a 'rollback', as defined in L1?
choices: Undoing every change made so far in a transaction, restoring the state from before it started
Making changes permanent
Retrying a failed write
Deleting the whole database
items.explanation: Rollback restores the exact state from before the transaction started.

items.prompt: What is a 'write-ahead log', as defined in L1?
choices: A durability mechanism: changes are logged before the system reports success, so a crash can still recover them
A list of every user who has ever written to the database
A log that's written only after a transaction commits
A performance optimization unrelated to durability
items.explanation: A write-ahead log is a durability mechanism: changes are written to it before success is reported.

items.prompt: When is a change written to the write-ahead log, relative to when the system reports success?
choices: After reporting success
Before reporting success
At the same exact instant, with no ordering guarantee
Only if the transaction is marked high-priority
items.explanation: The log write happens before success is reported — that ordering is what makes recovery possible.

items.prompt: If a transaction commits, does that mean rollback already happened?
choices: Yes, commit and rollback always happen together
No — commit and rollback are the two opposite outcomes; only one of them happens per transaction
Yes, rollback always happens first as a safety check
No, but only for transactions with more than one operation
items.explanation: Commit and rollback are mutually exclusive outcomes — exactly one happens per transaction.

items.prompt: Does a rollback restore the data to a brand-new state, or to the state from before the transaction started?
choices: A brand-new, specially computed state
The exact state from before the transaction started
Whatever state the last successful transaction left behind
There's no restoration — rollback just stops further writes
items.explanation: Rollback restores exactly the state from before the transaction began, as if it never ran.

items.prompt: Why would a write-ahead log help after a crash, compared to not having one?
choices: Because it lets the system recover a change that was already reported as successful, even if the crash happened right after
Because logs are always faster to write than normal data
Because it prevents crashes from happening at all
Because it automatically fixes any invariant violations
items.explanation: The log lets a reported success survive a crash — recovery can replay it even after the in-memory state is gone.

items.prompt: Is committing a transaction something that can be partially done — committed 'a little bit'?
choices: Yes, commits can be partial by design
No — commit only happens once every operation has succeeded; there's no partial commit
Yes, but only for transactions with exactly 2 operations
No, but only because databases forbid more than 1 operation per transaction
items.explanation: Commit is binary — it happens fully, once every operation has succeeded, or not at all.

items.prompt: If 'commit' means changes become permanent only once every operation has succeeded, what does that imply about a transaction where operation 1 succeeds and operation 2 is still running?
choices: Operation 1's effect is already permanent and visible
Nothing is permanent yet — commit hasn't happened, because not every operation has succeeded (operation 2 hasn't finished)
The transaction has already rolled back
Commit happens automatically after a fixed timeout regardless of operation 2
items.explanation: Commit is an all-at-once event gated on every operation succeeding — nothing is permanent until that gate passes.
items.reflection: Commit, rollback, and a durability log are three separate mechanical guarantees stacked on top of each other — one about when a result becomes final, one about undoing before that point, and one about that result surviving afterward. Can you think of a process in your own life (not software) where you'd want all three — a clear "point of no return," a way to back out before it, and some record that survives even if you forget or something goes wrong right after?

items.prompt: A system writes to its write-ahead log but never actually needs to read from it during normal operation — it just sits there. Does this mean the log is dead weight, or does it serve a purpose precisely because it's rarely read?
choices: Dead weight — if it's rarely read, it's not doing anything useful
It serves a purpose precisely because it's the thing recovery reads after a crash — being 'rarely read' just reflects that crashes are rare, not that the log is useless
It should be deleted to save space since it's rarely accessed
It's only useful for performance, not durability
items.explanation: The log's value is almost entirely in the rare crash case — being rarely read in normal operation doesn't mean it isn't essential.
items.reflection: Commit, rollback, and a durability log are three separate mechanical guarantees stacked on top of each other — one about when a result becomes final, one about undoing before that point, and one about that result surviving afterward. Can you think of a process in your own life (not software) where you'd want all three — a clear "point of no return," a way to back out before it, and some record that survives even if you forget or something goes wrong right after?

items.prompt: Compare: a system that rolls back cleanly on any failure but has no write-ahead log, versus a system with a write-ahead log but no rollback mechanism. Which one still risks ending up in a state that was never intended by any single transaction?
choices: The rollback-only system — without a log, a crash right after a reported success can simply erase that success, which is a different failure (lost durability), not a half-done transaction (lost atomicity) — so compare them on what EACH guarantee actually protects, not interchangeably
The log-only system, because logs always cause partial-write bugs
Neither — rollback and write-ahead logging are the same guarantee under two different names
Both, equally, because they solve the same problem
items.explanation: Rollback (atomicity) and the write-ahead log (durability) protect against different failures — a system missing the log can still lose an already-reported success to a crash.
items.reflection: Commit, rollback, and a durability log are three separate mechanical guarantees stacked on top of each other — one about when a result becomes final, one about undoing before that point, and one about that result surviving afterward. Can you think of a process in your own life (not software) where you'd want all three — a clear "point of no return," a way to back out before it, and some record that survives even if you forget or something goes wrong right after?

items.prompt: What does Consistency protect against, in L2's framing?
choices: Two requests reading each other's half-finished work
Data-level rules being broken, even for a single request acting alone
Crashes erasing already-reported successes
Requests running too slowly
items.explanation: Consistency is about data-level invariants holding, regardless of whether any other request is even running.

items.prompt: What does Isolation protect against?
choices: Data-level rules being violated by a single request
Two concurrent transactions seeing or interfering with each other's unfinished work
A crash erasing a committed result
An invalid orderId being submitted
items.explanation: Isolation is specifically about overlap between concurrent transactions.

items.prompt: If stock would go negative because of a single order's own bad math, with no other request involved, which property catches it?
choices: Isolation
Consistency
Durability
None — nothing catches single-request bugs
items.explanation: A single, solo request's invariant violation is Consistency's job, not Isolation's.

items.prompt: If two orders both read 'stock = 10' at the same time and both try to sell from it, which property is concerned with that overlap?
choices: Consistency
Atomicity
Isolation
Durability
items.explanation: Overlap between two in-flight transactions is exactly Isolation's concern.

items.prompt: According to L2's table, what breaks without Atomicity, using the stock/order example?
choices: Stock decrements, order insert fails — a partial write
Two concurrent orders both reading 10 in stock
A crash wiping out a reported success
Nothing — atomicity has no example
items.explanation: L2's table ties Atomicity directly to L1's partial-write bug.

items.prompt: True or false: Consistency only matters when multiple requests are running at the same time.
choices: True
False — consistency is about data-level rules holding true regardless of concurrency
items.explanation: Consistency applies even to a single transaction acting entirely alone.

items.prompt: Can a single, solo transaction (no concurrency at all) violate Consistency?
choices: No, consistency violations require at least two transactions
Yes — if its own operations would leave an invariant broken, consistency catches that regardless of concurrency
No, because consistency is just another name for isolation
Yes, but only if the transaction has more than 3 operations
items.explanation: A lone transaction can still violate an invariant purely through its own logic.

items.prompt: Which property is specifically about what happens 'when two requests touch the same data at the same time'?
choices: Consistency
Isolation
Durability
Atomicity
items.explanation: That framing is L2's definition of Isolation's concern.

items.prompt: A single order transaction, running completely alone with no other requests in flight, tries to insert an order for a customer ID that doesn't exist in the customers table. Which property is responsible for rejecting this, and why is it not Isolation even though only one transaction is involved?
choices: Isolation, because any rejection during a transaction is isolation's job by default

Consistency — enforcing that an order must point to a real customer is a data-level rule that must hold regardless of concurrency; Isolation only has something to say when multiple transactions overlap, and there's only one here
Durability, because the order would be lost on crash anyway
Atomicity, because the insert is the only operation in the transaction
items.explanation: No overlap exists in this scenario, so Isolation has nothing to say — the rule being enforced is a data-level invariant, which is Consistency's domain.
items.reflection: Consistency and Isolation are often confused because both "catch bad states," but one is about a single actor's own rules and the other is about actors interfering with each other. Where else have you seen this same split — a rule that applies even when you're acting completely alone, versus a problem that only exists because of overlap with someone else acting at the same time?

items.prompt: Two transactions run concurrently: Transaction A checks 'stock >= 3' and then decrements stock by 3; Transaction B does the identical check-then-decrement for its own order of 3, at nearly the same moment, both seeing stock = 3 before either commits. If both commit, stock goes to -3. Is this failure best described as a Consistency bug or an Isolation bug?
choices: A pure Consistency bug — the invariant 'stock >= 0' was violated
A pure Isolation bug — it only happens because of the overlap; each transaction's own invariant check (stock >= 3 before its own decrement) was individually correct against what it could see
Neither — this scenario is impossible in any real database
A pure Atomicity bug, since each transaction's own writes were all-or-nothing
items.explanation: Each transaction's own math was correct in isolation; the failure only exists because of the overlap — that's Isolation's gap, not a Consistency bug.
items.reflection: Consistency and Isolation are often confused because both "catch bad states," but one is about a single actor's own rules and the other is about actors interfering with each other. Where else have you seen this same split — a rule that applies even when you're acting completely alone, versus a problem that only exists because of overlap with someone else acting at the same time?

items.prompt: A system enforces every invariant it has (consistency is airtight) but allows transactions to freely read each other's uncommitted, in-progress writes (no isolation at all). Could such a system ever end up violating one of its own consistency rules in production, despite consistency being 'airtight' in isolation testing (one transaction at a time)?
choices: No — airtight consistency checks always hold regardless of concurrency

Yes — a consistency check run against data that includes another transaction's uncommitted (and possibly about-to-be-rolled-back) writes can pass based on data that never really existed, which is exactly the gap isolation is meant to close
No, because consistency checks are always re-run after every other transaction commits
Yes, but only if the invariant involves more than one table
items.explanation: Consistency checks run against whatever data they can see — if that data includes another transaction's uncommitted work, the check can pass based on data that may never actually become real.
items.reflection: Consistency and Isolation are often confused because both "catch bad states," but one is about a single actor's own rules and the other is about actors interfering with each other. Where else have you seen this same split — a rule that applies even when you're acting completely alone, versus a problem that only exists because of overlap with someone else acting at the same time?

items.prompt: In the lifecycle diagram, what happens right after 'Begin transaction'?
choices: Commit immediately
Run operation 1
Rollback by default
Nothing — begin is the final step
items.explanation: The diagram runs operation 1 right after begin, then operation 2, before reaching the commit/rollback decision.

items.prompt: According to the diagram, what are the only two possible endings for a transaction?
choices: Commit or rollback
Retry or crash
Pause or resume
Success or silent partial write
items.explanation: Every transaction ends in exactly one of two ways: commit or rollback.

items.prompt: Is rollback a special case bolted on afterward, or the transaction system's default response to failure?
choices: A special case added only for specific known bugs
The default response to any failure
Something that only happens if explicitly requested by the caller
Not part of the transaction system at all
items.explanation: Rollback is the default response to any failure, not a special case for particular bugs.

items.prompt: What makes isolation possible, according to L2?
choices: Nothing is visible to the rest of the system until commit
Every operation runs on a separate server
Rollback happens before every operation
Operations are executed in a random order
items.explanation: Keeping changes invisible until commit is exactly what makes isolation possible.

items.prompt: According to the timeline table, what can other requests see 'during work' (before commit or rollback)?
choices: The transaction's private, not-yet-final changes are invisible to them; they see only the old committed data
The transaction's private, not-yet-final changes, in full
A randomly chosen subset of the changes
Everything except the first operation
items.explanation: Other requests only see the old, committed data while a transaction's work is still in progress.

items.prompt: What can other requests see 'after rollback'?
choices: The original state, as if the failed attempt never ran
A partially-undone state
The transaction's final intended state
Whatever the first operation managed to write
items.explanation: Rollback restores exactly the original, pre-begin state.

items.prompt: Is 'is this only relevant to e-commerce' answered yes or no in L2?
choices: Yes, this is e-commerce-specific
No — any multi-write logical action faces the same shape of problem
Yes, but only for inventory systems specifically
The question isn't addressed in L2
items.explanation: L2 explicitly generalizes past e-commerce to any multi-write logical action.

items.prompt: Which other example does L2 give of a multi-write action facing the same shape of problem as orders/stock?
choices: Transferring money between two accounts
Printing a receipt
Logging in a user
Rendering a web page
items.explanation: L2 gives transferring money (debit one account, credit another) as a parallel example.

items.prompt: The lifecycle diagram shows operation 2 failing and the flow going straight to Rollback. At that point, has operation 1's effect already been undone somewhere upstream, or is undoing it exactly what the rollback step itself does?
choices: Already undone upstream, before rollback even runs

Undoing it is exactly what rollback does — up until that point, operation 1's effect exists only inside the transaction's private workspace, never visible outside it, and rollback is the moment that whole workspace gets discarded
Operation 1 is never actually affected by rollback at all
Rollback only undoes operation 2, never operation 1
items.explanation: Rollback is the single moment the entire private workspace — including operation 1's effect — gets discarded.
items.reflection: The lifecycle's core trick is deferring visibility until one final moment (commit), rather than letting partial progress leak out as it happens. Where else have you seen a process deliberately hide its in-progress state and reveal everything only at one final moment — a draft that's invisible until published, a vote count that's sealed until polls close?

items.prompt: A developer argues: 'Since nothing is visible until commit, I don't need to worry about ordering operations carefully inside a transaction — I can run them in any order and isolation will protect me.' What's wrong with that reasoning?
choices: Nothing is wrong — order truly doesn't matter inside a transaction

Isolation only governs visibility to OTHER transactions, not correctness within this one — if operation 2 depends on operation 1's result (e.g. checking stock after decrementing it), running them out of order still produces a wrong result even though nothing else can see it mid-transaction
Isolation guarantees operations always run in parallel regardless of order
Rollback makes operation order irrelevant because everything gets undone anyway
items.explanation: Isolation is about external visibility, not internal ordering correctness — a transaction can still produce a wrong result from its own operations running in the wrong order.
items.reflection: The lifecycle's core trick is deferring visibility until one final moment (commit), rather than letting partial progress leak out as it happens. Where else have you seen a process deliberately hide its in-progress state and reveal everything only at one final moment — a draft that's invisible until published, a vote count that's sealed until polls close?

items.prompt: Extend the money-transfer example L2 gives: debiting account A and crediting account B inside one transaction. If the transaction commits, but a completely separate, un-transacted audit-log write (outside this transaction) fails right after, is the original premise — 'can this ever be left half-done?' — still satisfied for the transfer itself?
choices: No — the transfer itself is still fully done (A debited, B credited, both committed together); the audit log failing is a different, separate action that was never part of this transaction's atomicity boundary in the first place
Yes, because any failure anywhere in the system means the whole operation is considered half-done
No, because transactions automatically include every write that happens near them in time
Yes, but only if the audit log write happens before the transfer commits
items.explanation: A transaction's atomicity boundary only covers what's actually inside it — a separate, un-transacted write failing afterward doesn't retroactively make the transfer itself half-done.
items.reflection: The lifecycle's core trick is deferring visibility until one final moment (commit), rather than letting partial progress leak out as it happens. Where else have you seen a process deliberately hide its in-progress state and reveal everything only at one final moment — a draft that's invisible until published, a vote count that's sealed until polls close?

items.prompt: In the sequence diagram, what does step 1 do?
choices: Inserts the order record
Decrements widget stock by 3
Rolls back the transaction
Checks the invariant
items.explanation: Step 1 in the diagram decrements widget stock by 3.

items.prompt: What does step 2 do, and does it succeed?
choices: Inserts the order; it succeeds
Inserts the order; it fails because orderId is missing
Decrements stock again; it succeeds
Rolls back step 1; it fails
items.explanation: Step 2 tries to insert the order but throws because orderId is missing.

items.prompt: After the failed request, what is stock.widget?
items.explanation: Stock dropped to 7 from the decrement, and nothing undid it.

items.prompt: After the failed request, what is orders.length?
items.explanation: The order insert never succeeded, so orders stays empty.

items.prompt: Why doesn't step 1's effect get undone automatically?
choices: Because step 1 and step 2 are two independent lines of code with nothing wrapping them to connect a failure in one to undoing the other
Because step 1 always succeeds no matter what
Because JavaScript automatically undoes failed operations
Because the database itself refuses to apply step 1 until step 2 is checked
items.explanation: With no boundary wrapping both steps, a failure in step 2 has no automatic effect on step 1's already-applied change.

items.prompt: Was either individual line of code (step 1 or step 2) buggy?
choices: Yes, step 1 had a bug
Yes, step 2 had a bug
No — the missing piece is a boundary treating both lines as one unit, not a bug in either line
Yes, both lines had bugs
items.explanation: Neither line was individually wrong — the missing piece is structural.

items.prompt: Is this diagram showing a different bug from L1's scenario, or the exact same one traced at the statement level?
choices: A completely different bug
The exact same bug from L1, traced to the statement level
A bug that only happens in JavaScript specifically
A bug that requires concurrency to occur
items.explanation: This is L1's exact bug, shown at the level of two individual statements.

items.prompt: What would need to exist for step 1 to be automatically undone when step 2 fails?
choices: Faster hardware
A transaction boundary wrapping both steps
A bigger stock count
Running step 2 before step 1 instead
items.explanation: A transaction boundary around both steps is exactly what's missing.

items.prompt: If the two steps were reordered — insert the order first, then decrement stock — and the stock decrement is the one that fails this time, would the resulting bug be structurally different from the one shown, or the same shape with the roles swapped?
choices: Structurally different — reordering fixes the bug
The same shape with the roles swapped: now the order record exists but stock was never decremented, which is just as inconsistent as the original bug, only the specific wrong state differs
It would no longer be possible for either step to fail

items.explanation: A global lock over-serializes — per-product locking is the minimal change that lets unrelated products proceed concurrently.
items.reflection: The lost-update bug is specifically about two independently-correct decisions combining into a wrong outcome — neither A nor B did anything wrong by itself. Where else have you seen two individually reasonable actions, taken without visibility into each other, combine into a result neither actor would have chosen on their own (two people editing the same shared document from a stale copy, two people spending from the same shared budget without checking the other's recent spend)?

items.prompt: Extend further: with a per-product lock in place, two orders are each for a bundle of the SAME two products (say, 1 widget + 1 gear each), and each order acquires the widget lock and the gear lock in a different order from the other. Is a per-product lock alone now sufficient to prevent all problems, or does a new failure mode appear?
choices: Per-product locks are now fully sufficient — no new issue can arise

A new failure mode appears: a deadlock — order 1 holds the widget lock and waits for the gear lock, while order 2 holds the gear lock and waits for the widget lock, and neither can proceed; per-product locking fixes the lost-update race but introduces a new class of problem (ordering/deadlock) that a single global lock never had
The per-product lock automatically merges into a single lock whenever two products are requested together
This scenario is impossible because bundles can only ever touch one product
items.explanation: Acquiring multiple per-resource locks in inconsistent order is the classic setup for deadlock — a new failure mode that a single global lock, despite its other costs, never has.
